clinicalPearls: Defined as incomplete development of the lung with a reduced number of airway generations, alveoli and pulmonary vessels, giving an abnormally low lung weight and volume for body size.
Primary (isolated) hypoplasia is rare; the majority of cases are secondary to an identifiable intrathoracic or extrathoracic cause.

Major secondary mechanisms include thoracic space restriction (congenital diaphragmatic hernia, effusion or hydrops, masses), oligohydramnios (renal agenesis or Potter sequence, prolonged rupture of membranes), thoracic cage constraint (skeletal dysplasias, neuromuscular disease) and reduced foetal breathing movements.
Normal lung growth requires adequate amniotic fluid volume, sufficient intrathoracic space and regular foetal breathing movements, particularly during the canalicular and saccular stages.
Affected neonates typically present with respiratory distress from birth, are difficult to ventilate and are prone to air leaks such as pneumothorax.
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn frequently coexists because the pulmonary vascular bed is both reduced in number and abnormally muscularised.
Antenatal predictors of severity in congenital diaphragmatic hernia include the lung-to-head ratio and the degree of liver herniation on ultrasound and foetal MRI.
Management is supportive with lung-protective ventilation, pulmonary vasodilators and treatment of the underlying cause, with extracorporeal support reserved for selected severe cases.
reference.pathophysiology: Normal lung growth depends on sufficient intrathoracic space, an appropriate volume of amniotic and intrapulmonary fluid maintaining distending pressure, and regular foetal breathing movements; interference with any of these during the critical canalicular and saccular phases arrests branching morphogenesis and alveolarisation. Space-occupying lesions and effusions compress the developing lung, oligohydramnios removes the distending fluid pressure and allows lung liquid to drain, and thoracic or neuromuscular constraint prevents the mechanical stretch that drives growth. The result is a lung with fewer bronchial divisions, fewer and simplified alveoli, and a diminished, abnormally muscularised vascular bed that predisposes to hypoxaemia and pulmonary hypertension after birth.
additionalDifferentials: Respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (both cause and differential)
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
Alveolar capillary dysplasia with misalignment of pulmonary veins
additionalInvestigations: Antenatal ultrasound with lung-to-head ratio and amniotic fluid assessment
Foetal MRI for lung volume estimation
Chest radiograph noting a small bell-shaped thorax and low lung volumes
Echocardiography to assess pulmonary hypertension and associated cardiac anomalies
Arterial blood gas and pre- and post-ductal saturation monitoring
Renal ultrasound and genetic or karyotype testing to identify the underlying cause
Post-mortem lung weight-to-body-weight ratio and radial alveolar count where applicable
redFlags: Severe refractory hypoxaemia and hypercapnia unresponsive to escalating support
Suprasystemic pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular failure
Inability to achieve adequate ventilation despite optimal settings, suggesting severe hypoplasia
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends chiefly on the severity of hypoplasia and its underlying cause: severe bilateral disease, as in Potter sequence, is frequently fatal, whereas milder secondary hypoplasia may improve with postnatal lung growth.
pitfalls: Attributing neonatal respiratory failure solely to surfactant deficiency and missing underlying hypoplasia.
Underestimating the contribution of pulmonary hypertension to hypoxaemia.
Using aggressive ventilation that causes barotrauma in small, non-compliant lungs.
Failing to search for the underlying renal, skeletal or diaphragmatic cause once hypoplasia is recognised.
Providing over-optimistic counselling before severity has been fully assessed.
